power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p ≤ 2.8 ", "p = 0.49"), Sentence = c("Across the 66 libraries, both correlated positively with endoscopic grade (Spearman correlation coefficient ρ = 0.66 and 0.65; p ≤ 2.8 × 10⁻⁹; Fig. 4a).", "CD in cohort 1 is the weakest cell: calprotectin did not track grade there (p = 0.49), although the stool score did (p = 0.044)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Gastrointestinal diagnosis and monitoring rely on colonoscopy, which requires anesthesia and a long wait, and non-invasive alternatives are lacking.

Here we show that whole-transcriptome sequencing of stool host RNA, recovering a median of 6,300 protein-coding genes across 285 libraries spanning colorectal cancer (CRC) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), precancerous lesions (APL), and normal samples, reads a census of the cells shed into the lumen.
In normal samples, epithelium supplies 81% and immune cells supply 11% of stool host mRNA transcripts; the immune cells' share rises in CRC and IBD, and B-and T-cell receptor clonotypes rise with it.

In this work, we show that CRC, IBD, and normal samples carry distinct transcriptome profiles, which a three-class model separates with an area under the curve of 0.94-0.96, and that within inflammatory bowel disease a 15-gene neutrophil score tracks endoscopic activity better than fecal calprotectin in the same stool.
Gastrointestinal diagnosis and monitoring rely heavily on colonoscopy, which requires bowel preparation and anesthesia, and carries a small procedural risk.

A patient presenting with nonred-flag gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea or bloating is worked up by exclusion-blood counts, C-reactive protein, stool culture, fecal calprotectin, celiac serologybefore colonoscopy settles whether the cause is neoplastic, inflammatory or functional 1, 2 .

text.text: The diagnostic pathway can take weeks to months.

Once inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is diagnosed, activity is monitored by repeat endoscopy or by fecal calprotectin, a single neutrophil protein that reports inflammation as one number and correlates only moderately with mucosal healing, particularly in Crohn's disease 3, 4 .

text.text: These two clinical problems share one missing measurement: a molecular readout of the state of the gut tissue and its immune response, obtainable repeatedly from a sample the patient can collect at home.
Stool contains that readout.

Epithelial cells exfoliate continuously along the entire tract, and immune cells that traffic into the mucosa are shed with them, so the human mRNA in stool integrates active biology across the intestine rather than reporting a single biopsy site or the systemic average that blood provides 5, 6 .

text.text: Recovering human RNA in stool is hard: most stool RNA is microbial, RNase activity is high, PCR inhibitors are abundant, and the matrix is hard to homogenize reproducibly 7, 8 .

text.text: The field has taken two routes around the microbial background.
The first is to sequence only chosen genes.
Huang et al. used amplicon sequencing (Foli-seq) of 543 genes and characterized immune dynamics in the healthy and inflamed gut 9 .
text.formatted: Huang et al. used amplicon sequencing (Foli-seq) of 543 genes and characterized immune dynamics in the healthy and inflamed gut <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Ghannam et al. used hybridization capture of a custom 1,507-transcript panel from stool RNA to separate active from quiescent Crohn's disease 10 .

text.text: These assays read the genes they were built to read: they cannot report a compartment that was not targeted, cannot assign transcripts to cell types across a whole reference atlas, and cannot be asked a new question without a new design.
The second route is poly(A) capture.

Using this approach, Halpern et al. recovered a median of 1,745 human genes per stool sample at ~20 million reads, and distinguished CRC patients from controls with a signal that mirrored the matched tumor tissue 11 .

text.text: These studies show the diagnostic potential of host mRNA in stool, but the genes they detect are a small fraction of the roughly twenty thousand protein-coding genes in the human genome, and their cohorts were either one disease at varying activity or one disease against healthy controls.
Whether the stool host transcriptome can tell two gastrointestinal diseases apart has not been explored.

Likewise, previous stool-mRNA studies have separated active IBD from remission using a classification model, but none has attempted to track the dynamic changes of different types of immune cells and immune repertoire as the disease severity of IBD increases.
Here, we developed a stool host RNA-seq protocol that detects more protein-coding genes than previously reported methods.
Using it, we generated 285 RNA-seq libraries from four clinical groups (normal, IBD, CRC, and APL) to address four questions.
First, which cells do the mRNA transcripts in stool come from?
Second, can adaptive immune signals, particularly T-cell and Bcell receptor (TCR and BCR) sequences, be detected in stool host RNA?
Third, can stool mRNA distinguish between different GI diseases, specifically CRC and IBD?
Fourth, can stool mRNA capture changes in immune cell populations across IBD severity, and so serve as a biomarker for disease monitoring?

We find that stool host RNA is a census of shed cells, comprising epithelial cells from along the gastrointestinal tract as well as innate and adaptive immune cells, and that it also captures TCR and BCR repertoires.

We further found that CRC and IBD leave distinct, separable transcriptional programs in this census, and that within IBD, neutrophil influx, the immune cell fraction, and the adaptive immune response all scale with disease severity and can be read from a single library.
The QC metrics of stool host transcriptome sequencing
We developed an RNA-seq protocol that efficiently isolates stool mRNA and converts it into an Illumina sequencing library (Fig. 1a).
text.formatted: We developed an RNA-seq protocol that efficiently isolates stool mRNA and converts it into an Illumina sequencing library (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: In brief, oligo(dT) probes capture the human mRNA specifically and leave the abundant microbial nucleic acids behind.
The protocol uses an optimized lysis buffer and conditions that release cellular RNA from human cells efficiently while protecting the mRNA from further degradation.

The oligo(dT) probes capture both the relatively intact cellular RNA and the more degraded cell-free RNA, together with optimized mRNA binding and elution conditions and a workflow that can easily scale with stool input.
Together, these improvements raised the quality of stool RNA-seq.

Compared with existing methods for profiling the stool host transcriptome, ours detects far more protein-coding genes: the median across the 285 libraries was 6,300 (Fig. 1b), almost double the largest number previously reported, even under a stringent definition (genes with ≥ 10 reads, after removing reads with mapping quality (MAPQ) < 30).

As a check, the median intergenic rate of the reads mapped to the human genome was only 0.7%, indicating very little DNA contamination.

We first asked which cell types the stool host mRNA originates from and in what proportions, because this determines which diseases, and at which sites, a stool mRNA test could surveil.
We used cell-type deconvolution to estimate the share of transcripts derived from each cell type.
A common pitfall of deconvolution is that cell types of the same lineage have very similar expression profiles, so their individual shares cannot be assigned accurately.

text.text: Can stool mRNA distinguish gastrointestinal diseases from one another, or does it only report how inflamed the gut is?

To answer this we performed principal-component analysis on the 2,000 most variable genes, setting aside the IBD libraries in endoscopic remission (n = 14) because a healed mucosa is expected to resemble Normal stool.
Plotting component scores by disease group, the dominant axis (PC1, 62% of variance) separated both CRC and IBD from Normal stool (single-component AUC 0.90 and 0.91).
The component that best separated CRC from IBD was PC6 (AUC 0.86); no other component reached 0.7.

Plotting PC1 against PC6 shows the separation of Normal, active IBD, and CRC libraries (Fig. 3a): this unsupervised decomposition already separates the libraries by diagnosis, which indicates that the signals distinguishing active IBD from CRC are strong.

Distinguishing IBD, CRC and Normal stool has direct clinical utility: for patients with mild gastrointestinal symptoms, a non-invasive stool test that flags likely IBD or CRC could triage them to colonoscopy and avoid weeks or months of waiting.
We therefore built a three-class multinomial logistic-regression model on 208 libraries (CRC 55, IBD 76, Normal 77; Methods).

Stool-based screening for CRC and APL is among the most widely used non-invasive stool tests.
We therefore asked whether a classifier built directly on the stool host transcriptome can detect CRC and APL.

We trained a two-class logistic-regression model on the 20 genes with the largest Welch t-statistic within each training fold, using five-fold cross-validation and CRC (n = 55), APL (n = 63), and Normal (n = 77) samples (Methods).
It separated CRC from Normal with AUC 0.969 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.94-0.99) and APL from Normal with AUC 0.713 (0.62-0.80).
The sensitivity is 90% for CRC and 42% for advanced adenomas at 90% specificity (Fig. 3i).

Better ways to monitor disease activity in IBD are an unmet clinical need.
The standard is endoscopy, and the only non-invasive alternative in routine use is the fecal calprotectin immunoassay, whose accuracy is limited, especially in Crohn's disease 4 .

text.text: We therefore asked whether stool host RNA can monitor IBD activity with better accuracy.

We took the 66 IBD libraries with an endoscopic grade evaluated within 30 days of stool collection and a recorded subtype-33 ulcerative colitis (UC) and 33 Crohn's disease (CD); remission 12, mild 17, moderate 17, severe 20-together with 24 healthy samples as a reference band.
The healthy samples are a subset of the Normal group that, in addition to a negative colonoscopy, showed no evidence of inflammation or other lesions (Methods).
We first examined the two genes encoding the calprotectin complex, S100A8 and S100A9, since fecal calprotectin is well established to rise during IBD flares.
Across the 66 libraries, both correlated positively with endoscopic grade (Spearman correlation coefficient ρ = 0.66 and 0.65; p ≤ 2.8 × 10⁻⁹; Fig. 4a).

text.text: We therefore defined a neutrophil panel of 15 genes that are highly and specifically expressed in neutrophils and took the mean z-score of their expression as a neutrophil score (Methods).

The score correlated with grade more closely than S100A8 or S100A9 alone (Spearman correlation coefficient ρ = 0.75) and separated each grade from the next with statistical significance (Fig. 4a; two-sided Mann-Whitney U, p = 0.012 for remission versus mild, 0.013 for mild versus moderate and 0.0011 for moderate versus severe).

text.text: To demonstrate the potential clinical utility, we compared the stool-mRNA panel with the conventional method, fecal calprotectin.

Because the number of IBD libraries in each endoscopic grade is small, a machine-learning model trained on this dataset would risk wide confidence intervals and over-fitting, so we took a biology-driven approach and used the neutrophil score directly as the stool-mRNA alternative to calprotectin.
The IBD libraries were split into two cohorts by the recruiting hospital, whose calprotectin reagents and instruments differ (Methods).

The stool-RNA neutrophil score tracked endoscopic grade more closely than calprotectin did on the identical samples, in both recruiting cohorts and in both subtypes (Fig. 4d; Supplementary Fig. 5): in UC, the Spearman correlation with endoscopic grade was ρ = 0.71 for the neutrophil score against 0.48 for calprotectin in cohort 1 (n = 12) and 0.68 against 0.39 in cohort 2 (n = 20); in CD, 0.53 against 0.19 in cohort 1 (n = 15) and 0.76 against 0.62 in cohort 2 (n = 16); and pooled across subtypes, 0.66 against 0.36 in cohort 1 (n = 27) and 0.75 against 0.11 in cohort 2 (n = 36; Fig. 4d).

Everything reported here is enabled by a stool host RNA-seq method that surveys the stool host transcriptome without targeting particular genes and that detects more human genes than any previously reported approach.
The first finding is a systematic account of the cells of origin of host RNA in stool, something never done systematically or unbiasedly before.

Normal stool is dominated by intestinal epithelium, whose colonocyte, goblet, enterocyte, Paneth and gastric markers are each individually recoverable and specific against a single-cell reference; the immune fraction is small and neutrophil-led; and lymphocyte transcripts sit near the detection floor.

Disease inverts the mixture toward immune cells, and the adaptive compartment becomes readable not only as transcripts but as assembled antigen receptors: these track their lineage genes, match receptors recorded in public databases and include the MAIT-like α chains expected at a mucosal surface.
To our knowledge, this is the first recovery of TCR and BCR sequences from stool host RNA.
We demonstrated three potential clinical applications of stool host transcriptome sequencing.
The first is differential diagnosis.

CRC, IBD and Normal stool carry distinct transcriptional signatures, and the genes that separate cancer from colitis resolve into canonical disease programs: Wnt signaling, stroma and proliferation on the cancer side, and an interferon-γ response on the colitis side.

A three-class model read on these features separated CRC, IBD and Normal stool with one-versus-rest AUCs of 0.94 to 0.96, which shows that stool host RNA carries the identity of the disease and not only the presence of inflammation.
To our knowledge, this is the first study showing that the stool host transcriptome can discriminate between different gastrointestinal diseases.
The second application is screening for advanced neoplasia.

A two-class model distinguished CRC from Normal at an AUC of 0.97; APL from Normal at 0.71, and it did so on hemoglobin, stromal and inflammatory transcripts rather than on the lesion's own epithelial program.
The census reports what a lesion sheds, and an adenoma sheds much less than CRC.
The third application is monitoring IBD activity.

A classifier on the 15-gene neutrophil score alone separated active disease from the quiescent gut at an AUC of 0.92, and the same libraries reported the infiltrate behind that score: the immune-cell share of transcripts, the neutrophil score and the B-cell and T-cell signature scores all rose with endoscopic grade, as did the number of productive BCR and TCR clonotypes.
The stool neutrophil score also tracked endoscopic grade more closely than the conventional fecal calprotectin measured on the same stool, in both recruiting cohorts and in both subtypes.

The correlation was weakest in Crohn's disease in cohort 1, as expected for a patchy transmural disease sampled from the lumen, and should be read as a boundary of the approach rather than a failure of the assay.
Several limitations apply.
The activity cohort is modest: 66 graded IBD libraries, 63 of them with a paired calprotectin.
Its grade axis pools UC and CD, which were graded with different instruments-the Mayo endoscopic subscore and SES-CD-that score different lesions and were mapped onto a single four-level band.

The subtypes also differ in extent, since UC is confined to the colon whereas CD usually involves the ileum and can involve any segment of the gut, so the endoscopic reference may not capture all the disease a stool sample integrates.
We pooled them because the number of libraries within each subtype is small, and the two are unevenly distributed across grades (19 of 33 UC libraries severe, 1 of 33 CD).

Detection of a marker is evidence that transcripts of that cell type are present, not a cell count, and the deconvolution reports shares of transcripts, which depend on the mRNA content of each lineage.

In this proof-of-principle study we have shown that stool host transcriptome sequencing recovers mRNA not only from the gut epithelium but also from immune cells, together with their antigen-receptor repertoire, and we have demonstrated its clinical potential in gastrointestinal differential diagnosis, CRC screening and the monitoring of IBD activity.

The same readout could serve diagnosis, prediction of drug response and disease monitoring across a wider range of gastrointestinal conditions, such as Clostridioides difficile infection and irritable bowel syndrome.

text.text: Fresh stool samples were collected by patients in fecal collection tubes, delivered to the hospital within 4 h, and stored at -80 °C. Human RNA was isolated from 1 g of stool per sample.
The method first lyses human cells in lysis buffer and enriches the human mRNA on oligo(dT) beads.

We quantified the extracted RNA by NanoDrop (concentration, A260/A280, and A260/A230), measured host RNA content by GAPDH amount using RT-qPCR (Takara OneStep Prime Script III RT-qPCR 2X Master mix (Takara Bio, part #RR601)), and stored it at -80 °C. The librarypreparation procedure specifies a total RNA concentration ≥100 ng µl⁻¹ (NanoDrop One C, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a GAPDH RT-qPCR Ct ≤31 as its input requirement for the downstream library preparation.
The isolated fecal RNA was converted into strand-specific, dual-indexed libraries with the Fast RNA-seq Lib Prep Kit V2 (ABclonal, China), using 16 PCR cycles and unique dual-index primers.
Libraries were sequenced as 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads on a NovaSeq 6000 to a median of 47 million clean reads (range 25-173 million) after adapter and quality trimming.
In Cohort 1, the calprotectin concentration was measured using the Fecal Calprotectin Detection Kit (Guangzhou Forreal Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).
In Cohort 2, the calprotectin concentration was measured using the BÜHLMANN fCAL ELISA (BUHLMANN, Switzerland).
Reads were processed with the RNA-seq pipeline: trimmed and quality-filtered with fastp 1.3.0 19 (default settings) and aligned to GRCh38 with STAR 2.7.11b 20 .

text.text: Cell types were clustered by average-linkage hierarchical clustering on cosine distance and the tree was cut at a distance of 0.15 (33  clusters).

A predefined list of twelve lineage merges, based on prior biological knowledge, was then applied in order, each joining the two clusters that held the named cell types and accepted only if the mean cosine distance between those clusters was ≤0.25 (all twelve were, at 0.16-0.24): tuft cells with colonocytes; microglia with macrophages; platelets with megakaryocytes; erythrocytes with erythrocyte progenitors; late spermatids with undifferentiated spermatogonia, then oocytes with late spermatids, giving one germ-cell cluster; Müller glia with astrocytes, then retinal ganglion cells, astrocytes and retinal horizontal cells each with brain excitatory neurons, giving one neural-glial cluster; and myonuclei, then thymic myoid cells, with cardiomyocytes, giving one striated-muscle cluster.

Six squamous cell types (esophageal apical, basal and suprabasal cells, basal and suprabasal keratinocytes, and ocular epithelial cells) were separated into a cluster of their own, because squamous cells reach stool by a different route from intestinal epithelium and pooling them with other epithelia obscures the dominant stool compartment.

Hepatocytes were left as the singleton produced by the cut: because a cluster signature is the mean of its members, merging hepatocytes into the columnar gastrointestinal cluster would allow hepatocyte-restricted genes to score as markers of the compartment that dominates stool, and would leave no separate column to absorb apolipoprotein transcripts that both intestine and liver produce (see Cluster-level deconvolution).
This procedure yielded 22 clusters (Supplementary Fig. 1; members in Supplementary Table 1).

text.text: Cluster signatures were the mean nCPM of member cell types.

Marker genes were selected at the cluster level on three criteria: (i) expression ≥10 nCPM in the highest-expressing cluster; (ii) that cluster accounting for ≥85% of the gene's summed cluster means; and (iii) expression ≥10 nCPM in at least 34% of that cluster's member cell types.

Criterion (iii) ensures that a marker describes the cluster rather than one of its members: criteria (i) and (ii) score only the contrast between clusters, and because a cluster profile is a member mean, a gene expressed by a single member of a large cluster otherwise appears perfectly specific.
The resulting marker pool comprised 488 gene-cluster assignments, 479 of whose genes were present in the stool matrix.
Clusters with fewer than five markers -the five singletons above and C22 (stromal and vascular cell types) -were excluded from the fit, leaving 16 of 22 clusters.

text.text: This weighting minimizes relative rather than absolute error, which is appropriate when the mismatch between a tissue reference and a stool library is multiplicative.

A fixed floor was used in place of the cross-validated dampening constant of the original method, which is selected for stability across gene subsets rather than for accuracy and did not improve any performance measure we examined.
The reported quantity is the transcript share: the fitted coefficients, renormalized to sum to one across clusters.

Transcript share is not a cell-fraction estimate, because conversion to cell fractions requires equal mRNA content per cell, an assumption that does not hold across epithelial cells, neutrophils and erythrocytes.

text.text: MAITlike α chains were defined as TRAV1-2 joined to any of these J segments or, irrespective of V assignment, a CDR3α containing DSNYQLI; only TRAJ33 was matched on sequence as well as on J assignment, because exonuclease trimming can shorten SNDYKLS to as little as YKLS.
Chains with and without TRAV1-2 are reported separately.
Invariant natural killer T-cell α chains (TRAV10-TRAJ18) were sought the same way; none was found.

The sign of each component is arbitrary and was fixed as follows: PC1 was flipped where necessary so that it correlated positively (Spearman) with the neutrophil score; for every other component, the gene with the largest absolute loading was identified and the component was flipped where necessary so that this gene's loading was positive.

text.text: The genes differentially expressed on each side (522 higher in CRC, 769 higher in IBD) were tested with Enrichr against all tested genes as background, and each program is the overlap of its term with that list: 11, 23, 16 and 57 genes (Enrichr adjusted P = 0.019, 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁰, 1.9 × 10⁻⁵ and 3.0 × 10⁻³⁹).

Because every member gene is selected by the contrast it annotates, the scores describe that contrast rather than provide independent evidence for it; they show whether the CRC-IBD difference is one axis or several programs.

A program score is the mean z-score of log₂(TMM-CPM + 1) over its genes, standardized jointly across the Normal, IBD and CRC libraries (77, 76 and 55); CRC and IBD were compared by two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, with Normal shown for reference.

text.text: Classifiers were fitted on log₂(TMM-CPM + 1) by selecting the 2,000 most variable genes, standardizing, and fitting L2-penalized logistic regression (multinomial for more than two classes; lbfgs solver, C = 1.0, balanced class weights, up to 4,000 iterations), with gene selection and standardization refitted within each training fold.

Cross-validation was five-fold, stratified by class and grouped by stool sample (scikit-learn 53 StratifiedGroupKFold), and was repeated with ten random fold assignments; point estimates are means over the ten.
